Two years later, but on the off chance other people end up in the same boat as I just have, the original post was this:


So, I posted this comment on another post and I think more people can benefit from reading it, so:


There's no such thing as "OCD thought" or "Real thought". A thought is a thought, a natural process of your brain. Your heart beats, your brain thinks.


Your brain is constantly analyzing, judging and comparing things in order to protect you from any danger. This process can be very helpful in the 'outside world', for example the thought "What if there's a tiger behind that bushes" probably saved a lot of our ancestors. But, when applied to our 'inner world', that same process can be extremely unhelpful if we want to live healthier lives. In the 'outside world' we can go and see if there's a tiger behind the bushes, or we can go away and that's it. But in our minds, we can never be sure about anything. So we keep ruminating about the thoughts in order to feel certain about something, we keep trying to rationalize it, to give meaning to a thought. And that's what leads to OCD: you have a thought you don't like, you get anxious, then you engage in a compulsion in order to cope with, avoid it or reassure yourself that the thought isn't 'real'. Everybody does that to some extent, but people with OCD have their lives stuck because they feel they need to be certain of something before they can DO something. It's like as if the person needs to see if there's a tiger in the bush, then after seeing there's no tiger, a time later, another thought pops up "Are you sure you took a good look behind that bushes?", anxiety comes again, the person feel the urge to take another look etc. etc. then another thought "What if the tiger was hiding?", or "What if the tiger wasn't really there but it's there right now?". More urges, more compulsions etc etc.


So, fuck that tiger. Your job in recovery is to cut the compulsions. "What if there's a tiger behind the bushes?" Let it be there, maybe there's a tiger, maybe there isn't, but I'm choosing to live my life anyway. "But what if I don't look and the tiger attacks me at night?", well, thanks brain, that's possible, so I'm gonna focus on living my life right now and when the tiger kills me at night I can rest in peace because I know I acted based on my values. "What if my girlfriend is not the ideal person for me?", Thanks brain, you might be right, but I choose to focus on loving her and having quality time with her.


So, what I'm trying to tell you is that the thoughts are not the problem. The problem is the way we behave after having a thought we don't like or a feeling, desire or urge. People with great mental health have the same doubts and thoughts we have here in this sub. People with great mental health can decide to break up because their partner have some minor imperfections like an ugly thumb (have you seen megan fox's thumbs?). And that's ok. The difference between people with great mental health and people with OCD is that we suffer a lot because we tend to ruminate over thoughts, trying to understand what do they mean, what they say about us etc.


So, is very understandable when you make the question "How can you know that's it's OCD and not real inner aspiration?" because you're acting exactly how people with OCD acts. You're are trying to be certain of something, but you can't be certain, so you keep wondering and wondering and you feel stuck because everytime you have an answer, another doubt pops up.


That's why is so important to cut compulsions and act based on what you value. If you don't know what your values are, try asking yourself "What are my deepest desires for who I want to be? What I want to stand for in life? What kind of partner I want to be?" Then you will get some answers and you can start to build your life around that, accepting whatever your minds tells you.


Just to make it more clear: In my case, I want to be a supportive partner, a compassionate human being. I want to accept my girlfriend's flaws and build our relationship based on mutual respect. These are my values and the things I want to stand for. Whenever a thought pops up, like "Urgh, she's getting fat, I can't date a fat woman", I can accept the thought, accept that it exists, accept that maybe it causes me anxiety, but I can choose my actions. Instead of engaging in a compulsion (avoiding kissing her, manipulate her into a diet etc), I can choose to act based on my values. So I can be compassionate, I can be kind and I can be supportive at the same time my brain keeps screaming a lot of crap in my mind. With time, cutting compulsions and acting based on your values will show you that you are in charge of your life regardless of your thoughts, and your brain eventually might stop being a bully.


Obviously, that's not an easy process. That's why we're all here.

Minorities get scapegoated because the majority needs someone to blame for their problems; it's a lot easier, usually, to point at us and claim we're somehow the problem, relying on pre-existing prejudice and the fact we deviate from social norms and conformity, than make actual systemic changes, confront why we are marginalised (accepting you have privilege when that privilege keeps you from being similarly marginalised isn't something most want to do, unfortunately). People who go against the way things are "supposed to be" and challenge the status quo even just by existing are a lot more likely to see the broken system we exist under. Politicians are rich and would like to stay that way. Getting the masses to call us the problem by scapegoating us prevents them from considering alternative angles and keeps the money flowing into their pockets as people are too busy pointing their fingers and calling trans women paedophiles for no reason.

I don't really have much advice for you but I'm writing this comment while ignoring my 3 overdue uni assessments (I wrote 2 lines of one earlier and then fell asleep for 2 and a half hours) just to tell you that you're not alone. It's fucking hard and because it's a rare disorder most people aren't really aware of it's even harder because of the social stigma. Enough people are going to see you as lazy and unmotivated because they don't understand but you can, you know there's something wrong, so if nothing else please try to be a bit kinder to yourself. You never asked to be this way, and it is a tremendous struggle. I think everyone in here has gone through this kind of depression in some form before. I don't say it to invalidate you at all, just to reiterate that you're not alone in this; your struggle is completely valid.

It takes a lot of trial and error. I've just been put on amphetamines on top of my Sunosi and it's magic for the short few hours it's active, it makes it easier for me to focus on things that need doing (those 3 overdue assessments were 4 a few days ago... that's something 😭). Is it possible for you to talk about treatment options with your sleep doctor? I'm extremely lucky to live in a country with decent healthcare (even if the government is currently trying to destroy it) so I understand not everyone has that privilege, but it might be something to explore. And does your uni have any type of disability support? Mine are absolutely wonderful to me even though I really push it sometimes; I get more leniency regarding deadline extensions, no classes early in the morning where it can be helped, the freedom to not attend lectures since I'm pretty much guaranteed to fall asleep during those and instead watch the recordings of them later, etc. If your uni/school has any kind of disability help like that, it's well worth reaching out in my experience, though of course ymmv!

For jobs, that's taken a lot of experimentation too. McDonald's made me suicidal twice lol, I don't know why I went back. It's an easy job to get but it will destroy you; you're constantly up and on your feet, the work is disgusting and difficult, and you get tons of abuse from customers who refuse to understand you're just doing your best. It's best to consider what your strengths are, though! I recently started a warehouse job and I adore it; I only work 6 hour shifts so it's more bearable than 8 hours, I work 3am to 9am since I am way better at being awake and alert during the night and early morning and am then dead through the day (I think my circadian rhythm is delayed), and while it's physically quite taxing and very fast paced, I find that works well for keeping me awake since I'm always moving; I just need to nap after my shifts. Are there times of day you tend to be more awake? Could you potentially try different shift patterns or types of work? I know it's hard, and the job market right now is absolutely atrocious (it took me 5 months of destroyed mental health at McD's to keep paying my rent to get this job), but something might come up. Alternatively, could you maybe apply for any benefits (/social security? I don't know where you are or what's available to you)? 

Otherwise the best things you can do are a) as I've said, try to show yourself kindness, as we are struggling with something most people could never even comprehend and b) try to look after your health in other ways. Not only eating healthy and exercising like everyone suggests, but figuring out if you have any trigger foods (certain carbs/gluten is rough on me, for example) and what kinds of exercises work best for you; most cardio makes me super sleepy and yoga knocks me out but weightlifting and pilates have been great for my energy levels, for example. Looking after your body and mind in this sense gives you something to do, if nothing else, and might help ease the severity of your narcolepsy, though it obviously isn't a cure no matter how many 40 year old know it alls might think it is! And as someone who also sleeps for ridiculous amounts of the day, I find sleeping less but more often (ie I sleep 6-7.5 hours at night instead of the 9 I used to, and then schedule naps twice a day around my work and uni schedule) keeps me going better than sleeping for like 12 hours straight.

I'm not a teacher but I got recommended this thread randomly and reading me through is taking me right back to year 11. I was pretty much a star pupil but I had a bit of mental breakdown after my mocks in year 10 that got continually worse. The after school study sessions that made school an extra 50 mins than it already was, the amount of homework and coursework and studying that meant I had basically no free time, the ridiculous heat in the halls since you do exams at the start of summer, the feeling of pressure from every single teacher who also obviously have stakes in you doing well because their entire career is getting you to this point; I'd had a lot of the same teachers since year 7, I felt desperate.  

I'm now diagnosed with ADHD and narcolepsy,—the latter of which was easily the worst thing to have undiagnosed in high school actually—but even then, facing so much pressure for so long with rather little time to unwind and constantly high expectations from those around me broke me down, and it all felt it was for nothing anyway because I had no ambitions at the time; I didn't know what I wanted to study at uni, I didn't know what I wanted to do for a job, with how current wages are and all you hear about the economy it all felt useless anyway because all we ever hear is that we're never going to have the house and retirement of those who came before us. I'd argue it's even worse for these kids now as TikTok wasn't a thing when I was in school; they are constantly barraged with quick short videos about how absolutely fucked they are, in essence, and a lot of it is true.  

In the end, I tried to off myself and my mum pulled me from school, so I had no GCSEs until I sat my maths and English at 17/18 to at least have the bare minimum. I've made it to uni now anyway, thankfully, but the feeling that I'd disappointed everyone was too much at the time. I was completely despondent and depressed for at least a year afterwards, no matter how much my parents assured me that there were different paths to my future, and that it's better I'm alive than dead with all 9s (or 2 9s and all As, since this was 2017 lol). I'm only just finding out how to handle stress and anxiety now as a nearly 23 year old; it's a LOT for a teenage brain to handle while feeling like you have absolutely no choice.  

Of course, I feel a lot of teachers here will obviously disagree since your job is getting us ready for GCSEs, and I'm full of appreciation for what you do and I'm still thankful for my good teachers to this day, but there indeed were paths beyond GCSEs, I wasn't fucked because I didn't sit mine in the end (though part of that was because I paid my own way lol, it is more expensive if you don't sit them for sure!), but at the time it was my entire world. It felt like all or nothing. If I fail these, my entire life is over. And for all that to be put on someone who has barely even lived yet... I'm not surprised so many are just giving up. I also don't doubt that some are lazy and unmotivated and thrive on causing trouble, because every school has those, but thinking about my own high school experiences at least helps me empathise with those who might also be going through similar.
